claim: Mouse TRPA1 localizes preferably into cholesterol-rich domains.
source: Using total internal reflection fluorescence microscopy and density gradient centrifugation we found that mouse TRPA1 localizes preferably into cholesterol-rich domains
evidence: The claim is supported by experimental data from TIRF microscopy and density gradient centrifugation experiments described in the manuscript.

claim: Cholesterol depletion decreases mTRPA1 channel sensitivity to chemical agonists.
source: functional experiments revealed that cholesterol depletion decreases channel sensitivity to chemical agonists
evidence: The claim is supported by functional experiments measuring channel responses to agonists after cholesterol depletion.

claim: Two structural motifs in transmembrane segments 2 and 4 are involved in mTRPA1-cholesterol interactions.
source: we identified two structural motifs in transmembrane segments 2 and 4 involved in mTRPA1-cholesterol interactions
evidence: The claim is supported by mutagenesis experiments and in silico docking simulations identifying CRAC motifs.

claim: CRAC motifs in TM2 and TM4 are necessary for normal agonist sensitivity of mTRPA1.
source: we identified two structural motifs in transmembrane segments 2 and 4 involved in mTRPA1-cholesterol interactions that are necessary for normal agonist sensitivity
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data showing that mutations in CRAC motifs alter agonist sensitivity.

claim: CRAC motifs in TM2 and TM4 are necessary for normal plasma membrane localization of mTRPA1.
source: we identified two structural motifs in transmembrane segments 2 and 4 involved in mTRPA1-cholesterol interactions that are necessary for normal agonist sensitivity and plasma membrane localization
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy data showing altered membrane distribution patterns in CRAC mutants.

claim: TRPA1 is a Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channel.
source: The Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channel TRPA1 is arguably the most versatile of such receptors expressed in sensory nerve fibers (Pedersen et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Paulsen et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is expressed in sensory nerve fibers.
source: The Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channel TRPA1 is arguably the most versatile of such receptors expressed in sensory nerve fibers (Pedersen et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Paulsen et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is expressed in skin keratinocytes.
source: The Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channel TRPA1 is arguably the most versatile of such receptors expressed in sensory nerve fibers (Pedersen et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Paulsen et al., 2015), skin keratinocytes (Anand et al., 2008; Atoyan et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is expressed in airway epithelial cells.
source: The Ca2+-permeable non-selective cation channel TRPA1 is arguably the most versatile of such receptors expressed in sensory nerve fibers (Pedersen et al., 2005; Kobayashi et al., 2005; Ji et al., 2008; Paulsen et al., 2015), skin keratinocytes (Anand et al., 2008; Atoyan et al., 2009) and airway epithelial cells (Nassini et al., 2012)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 has been implicated in sensory pathophysiology as a detector of thermal stimuli.
source: TRPA1 has been implicated in sensory pathophysiology as detector of thermal (Story et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2013; Karashima et al., 2009; Hamada et al., 2008; Moparthi et al., 2016; Moparthi et al., 2014; Survery et al., 2016; Viswanath et al., 2003; Kwan et al., 2006; Vandewauw et al., 2018) and mechanical (Kwan et al., 2006; Kindt et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2008; Kwan et al., 2009) stimuli
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 has been implicated in sensory pathophysiology as a detector of mechanical stimuli.
source: TRPA1 has been implicated in sensory pathophysiology as detector of thermal (Story et al., 2003; Chen et al., 2013; Karashima et al., 2009; Hamada et al., 2008; Moparthi et al., 2016; Moparthi et al., 2014; Survery et al., 2016; Viswanath et al., 2003; Kwan et al., 2006; Vandewauw et al., 2018) and mechanical (Kwan et al., 2006; Kindt et al., 2007; Zhang et al., 2008; Kwan et al., 2009) stimuli
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is activated by an extremely wide variety of noxious chemicals.
source: However, this channel is best known for being activated by an extremely wide variety of noxious chemicals (Nilius and Appendino, 2013; Nilius et al., 2011; Zygmunt and Högestätt, 2014; Startek et al., 2019b)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is activated by electrophilic compounds such as allyl isothiocyanate (AITC) and cinnamaldehyde.
source: For instance, TRPA1 is activated by electrophilic compounds such as allyl isothiocyanate (AITC) and cinnamaldehyde (Bandell et al., 2004; Bautista et al., 2005; Hinman et al., 2006; Macpherson et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is activated by non-electrophilic compounds including bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS).
source: This channel is also activated by numerous non-electrophilic compounds, some of which have been proposed to act by inducing mechanical disturbances in the plasma membrane, for example bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) (Meseguer et al., 2014; Soldano et al., 2016; Startek et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPA1 is activated by trinitrophenol and chlorpromazine.
source: This channel is also activated by numerous non-electrophilic compounds, some of which have been proposed to act by inducing mechanical disturbances in the plasma membrane, for example bacterial lipopolysaccharides (LPS) (Meseguer et al., 2014; Soldano et al., 2016; Startek et al., 2018), trinitrophenol and chlorpromazine (Hill and Schaefer, 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The function of TRPA1 can be regulated by the surrounding lipid environment.
source: Thus, it can be hypothesized that the function of TRPA1 can be regulated by the surrounding lipid environment (Startek et al., 2019a)
evidence: The claim is presented as a hypothesis supported by a citation.

claim: The responses of rat trigeminal neurons to AITC and formaldehyde are significantly impaired by pretreatment with sphingomyelinase.
source: It was recently reported that the responses of rat trigeminal neurons to the electrophilic agonists AITC and formaldehyde are significantly impaired by pretreatment with the lipid raft destabilizer sphingomyelinase (SMase), or with the cholesterol scavenger methyl β-cyclodextrin (MCD) (Sághy et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The responses of rat trigeminal neurons to AITC and formaldehyde are significantly impaired by pretreatment with methyl β-cyclodextrin (MCD).
source: It was recently reported that the responses of rat trigeminal neurons to the electrophilic agonists AITC and formaldehyde are significantly impaired by pretreatment with the lipid raft destabilizer sphingomyelinase (SMase), or with the cholesterol scavenger methyl β-cyclodextrin (MCD) (Sághy et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A carboxamido-steroid that disrupts lipid rafts reduced TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx in CHO cells transfected with the human isoform.
source: Furthermore, a carboxamido-steroid shown to disrupts lipid rafts reduced TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx in CHO cells transfected with the human isoform and in rat sensory neurons (Sághy et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: A carboxamido-steroid that disrupts lipid rafts reduced TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx in rat sensory neurons.
source: Furthermore, a carboxamido-steroid shown to disrupts lipid rafts reduced TRPA1-mediated Ca2+ influx in CHO cells transfected with the human isoform and in rat sensory neurons (Sághy et al., 2018)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: mTRPA1-mCherry colocalizes with lipid raft marker cholera toxin B in HEK293T cells.
source: With the use of total internal reflection fluorescence (TIRF) microscopy we found a population of highly mobile vesicular structures near the cellular membrane containing both mTRPA1-mCherry and the lipid raft marker cholera toxin B (Figure 1A and B, Video 1)
evidence: The claim is supported by TIRF microscopy data shown in Figure 1.

claim: The dynamic colocalization score of TRPA1 and lipid raft marker is 89%.
source: The colocalization of TRPA1 and lipid raft marker was analyzed as previously described (Ghosh et al., 2016), yielding a high dynamic colocalization score of 89% (n = 11)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantitative analysis of colocalization data.

claim: The introduction of the mCherry tag into the C-terminus did not influence TRPA1 responses to AITC.
source: The introduction of the mCherry tag into the C-terminus did not influence TRPA1 responses to its electrophilic agonist AITC, as the half-maximal effective concentration for wild type (WT) mTRPA1 and mTRPA1-mCherry were not significantly different (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A and B)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data comparing WT and mCherry-tagged channels.

claim: Channel activation by thymol was unaffected by the mCherry tag.
source: Moreover, channel activation by the non-electrophilic agonist thymol (100 or 300 µM) was also unaffected by the mCherry tag (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing responses to thymol.

claim: Flotillin-2 and plasma membrane gangliosides are markers of lipid rafts.
source: Both flotillin-2 and membrane gangliosides are markers of lipid rafts (Bickel et al., 1997; Zhao et al., 2011; Yu et al., 2011)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Na/K-ATPase localizes mainly outside lipid raft domains.
source: whereas Na/K-ATPase localizes mainly outside these domains (Storey et al., 2007)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: The highest flotillin-2 concentration is found in the 30% OptiPrep fractions (fractions 3 and 4).
source: We found the highest flotillin-2 concentration in the 30% OptiPrep fractions (fractions 3 and 4; Figure 2A)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2A.

claim: TRPA1-mCherry was enriched in the 30–35% gradients.
source: TRPA1-mCherry was also enriched in the 30–35% gradients confirming our previous observations from the TIRF microscopy (Figure 2A,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MCD treatment reduced the partition of mTRPA1-mCherry into lipid rafts.
source: A 45 min MCD treatment reduced the partition of mTRPA1-mCherry into lipid rafts (fractions 3 and 4), shifting the channel localization to non-raft fractions (Figure 2D,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western blot data after MCD treatment shown in Figure 2.

claim: MCD treatment reduces flotillin-2 and ganglioside levels in the DRM.
source: Flotillin-2 and ganglioside levels were reduced in the DRM (Figure 2D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by Western and dot blot data shown in Figure 2.

claim: MCD treatment at concentrations used should remove 30–50% of total cholesterol from cellular membranes.
source: Since the MCD concentration range used in our experimental conditions should remove 30–50% of total cholesterol from the cellular membranes (Hao et al., 2007; Levitt et al., 2009; Rodal et al., 1999; Pontier et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: 55.3% of DRG neurons responded to 30 µM AITC in control conditions.
source: In control conditions, 55.3% of neurons responded to 30 µM AITC, with an average increase in intracellular Ca2+ concentration (Δ[Ca2+]) of about 500 nM (Figure 3A,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data from DRG neurons shown in Figure 3.

claim: MCD pretreatment did not affect the percentage of neurons responding to AITC but significantly reduced the response amplitude.
source: After the MCD pretreatment the percentage of neurons responding to AITC was not different, but the responses were significantly smaller (Figure 3B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data comparing control and MCD-treated neurons.

claim: MCD did not affect the responses to high K+ in DRG neurons.
source: In contrast, MCD did not affect the responses to high K+, suggesting that neither the cell viability nor the excitability were altered
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data measuring responses to high K+.

claim: The responses to capsaicin were 27% smaller in MCD-pretreated DRG cells.
source: The responses to the TRPV1 agonist capsaicin were 27% smaller in MCD-pretreated cells (Figure 3C), confirming the reported modulation of TRPV1 by cholesterol (Sághy et al., 2015; Liu et al., 2006; Szoke et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data and citations to previous literature.

claim: MCD decreases the amplitude of Ca2+ responses to 300 µM thymol in DRG neurons.
source: Other experiments showed that MCD also decrease the amplitude of Ca2+ responses to 300 µM thymol and confirmed the invariance of the responses to high K+ and the reduction of the effect of capsaicin (Figure 3D,E,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3.

claim: SMase reduced the responses to AITC in DRG neurons.
source: SMase reduced the responses to AITC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C) and thymol, but did not significantly affect the responses to high K+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMase reduced the responses to thymol in DRG neurons.
source: SMase reduced the responses to AITC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C) and thymol, but did not significantly affect the responses to high K+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: SMase did not significantly affect the responses to high K+ in DRG neurons.
source: SMase reduced the responses to AITC (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A,B,C) and thymol, but did not significantly affect the responses to high K+ (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D,E)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1.

claim: The responses of CHO-mTRPA1 cells to AITC and thymol were reduced by pretreatment with either MCD or SMase.
source: As found in DRG neurons, the responses of CHO-mTRPA1 cells to AITC and thymol were reduced by the pretreatment with either MCD or SMase (Figure 3—figure supplement 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by calcium imaging data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2.

claim: The effects of MCD and SMase on TRPA1 responses were dependent on their concentrations.
source: These effects were dependent on the MCD and SMase concentrations (Figure 3—figure supplement 3)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 3.

claim: The CRAC motif consists of a short linear amino acid sequence: (L/V)-X1-5-(Y)-X1-5-(K/R).
source: One of them is the Cholesterol Recognition/interaction Amino acid Consensus (CRAC) motif, which in its first definition consisted of a short linear amino acid sequence composed of a branched apolar Leu or Val residue followed by a 1–5 any residue segment, then a Tyr residue followed by another 1–5 any residue segment and finally a basic Lys or Arg residue: (L/V)-X1-5-(Y)-X1-5-(K/R) (Fantini and Barrantes, 2013; Fantini et al., 2016)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature defining the CRAC motif.

claim: The extended definition of the CRAC motif is: (L/V)-X1-5-(Y/F/W)-X1-5-(K/R).
source: Recently, an extended definition of the CRAC motif was introduced, following the discovery that other aromatic residues such as Phe or Trp can interact with cholesterol (Fantini et al., 2016). Thus, the CRAC motif can now be described with the sequence: (L/V)-X1-5-(Y/F/W)-X1-5-(K/R)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Five possible CRAC motifs were identified in mTRPA1, four in TM2 and one in TM4.
source: We identified five possible CRAC motifs, four of which are located in TM2 and one in TM4 (Figure 4A,B)
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis shown in Figure 4.

claim: CRACs 2, 3, 4 and 5 are highly conserved throughout mammalian evolution.
source: Conservation analysis revealed that among these five motifs CRACs 2 (780-VFLSSIFGYCK-790), 3 (782-LSSIFGYCK-790), 4 (782-LSSIFGYCK-790) and 5 (850-LLYLQR-855) (residue numbering corresponding to mTRPA1) are highly conserved throughout mammalian evolution
evidence: The claim is supported by sequence alignment analysis across 24 mammalian species.

claim: WT mTRPA1 responded to AITC with an EC50 of 11.8 ± 2.5 µM in control conditions.
source: Cells transfected with WT mTRPA1 responded in control conditions to AITC with an effective concentration (EC50) of 11.8 ± 2.5 µM and a maximal intracellular [Ca2+] increase (Δ[Ca2+]Max) of 0.79 ± 0.4 µM
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from calcium imaging experiments.

claim: MCD pretreatment increased the EC50 of WT mTRPA1 for AITC by 5-fold.
source: In cells pretreated with MCD the EC50 was 5-fold higher and the Δ[Ca2+]Max was 40% of that obtained in control cells
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data comparing control and MCD-treated conditions.

claim: Mutations V780A and F786A in TM2 resulted in higher EC50 values than WT in control conditions.
source: In contrast, mutations V780A and F786A in TM2 (CRAC 2) resulted in EC50 values in control conditions that are higher than for WT and the pretreatment with MCD did not further increase the EC50 or decrease the Δ[Ca2+]Max values (Figure 5B,C,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from mutant channels shown in Figure 5.

claim: MCD pretreatment did not further increase the EC50 or decrease the Δ[Ca2+]Max values for V780A and F786A mutants.
source: In contrast, mutations V780A and F786A in TM2 (CRAC 2) resulted in EC50 values in control conditions that are higher than for WT and the pretreatment with MCD did not further increase the EC50 or decrease the Δ[Ca2+]Max values (Figure 5B,C,F)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data comparing control and MCD-treated mutant channels.

claim: Mutant L850A displayed a very large EC50 and small Δ[Ca2+]Max in control conditions compared to WT.
source: Mutant L850A in TM4 (CRAC 5) displayed a very large EC50 and small Δ[Ca2+]Max (0.24 ± 0.02 µM) in control conditions in comparison with the WT channel, and the MCD treatment did not affect these values (Figure 5D,F; Δ[Ca2+]Max = 0.20 ± 0.02 µM)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from the L850A mutant shown in Figure 5.

claim: MCD treatment did not affect the EC50 or Δ[Ca2+]Max values for the L850A mutant.
source: Mutant L850A in TM4 (CRAC 5) displayed a very large EC50 and small Δ[Ca2+]Max (0.24 ± 0.02 µM) in control conditions in comparison with the WT channel, and the MCD treatment did not affect these values (Figure 5D,F; Δ[Ca2+]Max = 0.20 ± 0.02 µM)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data comparing control and MCD-treated L850A mutant.

claim: Mutation Y852A resulted in a 60% increase of the EC50 in control conditions compared to WT.
source: Finally, mutation Y852A resulted in a 60% increase of the EC50 (Figure 5E,F) and a ~ 50% reduction of the Δ[Ca2+]Max (0.37 ± 0.02 µM) in control conditions with respect to the corresponding values of the WT channel
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data from the Y852A mutant shown in Figure 5.

claim: MCD treatment did not affect the sensitivity of the Y852A mutant.
source: As for L850A, the MCD treatment did not affect the sensitivity of the Y852A mutant (Figure 5E,F; Δ[Ca2+]Max = 0.32 ± 0.01 µM)
evidence: The claim is supported by dose-response data comparing control and MCD-treated Y852A mutant.

claim: Residues V780 and F786 in TM2 and L850 and Y852 in TM4 are crucial in the regulation of TRPA1 activity by cholesterol.
source: Taken together, these results show that residues V780 and F786 in TM2 and L850 and Y852 in TM4 are crucial in the regulation of TRPA1 activity by cholesterol
evidence: The claim is inferred from the functional data showing that mutations in these residues affect cholesterol-dependent regulation.

claim: Cholesterol was not able to dock to the model structure of the whole mTRPA1 channel due to steric hindrance.
source: We found that, due to steric hindrance, cholesterol was not able to dock to any of the transmembrane domains of our model structure of the whole mTRPA1 channel
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico docking simulations.

claim: Two cholesterol binding sites were identified in TM2 and two in TM4 when docking simulations were performed with individual transmembrane domains in vacuum.
source: On the other hand, when docking simulations were performed with individual transmembrane domains in vacuum we identified two cholesterol binding sites in TM2 and two other sites in TM4 (Figure 6C,D)
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico docking simulations shown in Figure 6.

claim: In TM2, the binding site containing V780 has higher affinity for cholesterol than the one containing F786.
source: Estimations of the interaction energy indicate that in TM2 the binding site containing V780 seems to have higher affinity for cholesterol than the one containing F786 (Figure 6E: ΔG for WT site one is more negative than for WT site 2)
evidence: The claim is supported by binding energy calculations shown in Figure 6E.

claim: The two binding sites in TM4 are almost energetically indistinguishable.
source: In contrast, the two binding sites in TM4 are almost energetically indistinguishable (Figure 6F: very similar ΔG for WT)
evidence: The claim is supported by binding energy calculations shown in Figure 6F.

claim: V780 and L850 interact with the hydrocarbon tail of cholesterol.
source: V780 and L850 interact with the hydrocarbon tail of cholesterol, whereas the aromatic residues F786 and Y852 interact with the hydrocarbon rings of the α-face of the molecule
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico docking simulations.

claim: F786 and Y852 interact with the hydrocarbon rings of the α-face of cholesterol.
source: V780 and L850 interact with the hydrocarbon tail of cholesterol, whereas the aromatic residues F786 and Y852 interact with the hydrocarbon rings of the α-face of the molecule
evidence: The claim is supported by in silico docking simulations.

claim: Single mutations of CRAC residues affect the binding energy of their own site but not of the neighboring one.
source: We also found that in silico single mutations of these residues affect the binding energy of their own site but not of the neighboring one (Figure 6E,F), further supporting the notion that cholesterol molecules can bind independently to each of the four sites
evidence: The claim is supported by binding energy calculations for mutant channels shown in Figure 6.

claim: Mutations of F786 and Y852 produce larger reductions in cholesterol binding energy than mutations of V780 and L850.
source: The calculations also show that the mutations of the amino acids F786 and Y852 produce larger reductions in cholesterol binding energy than the mutations of V780 and L850
evidence: The claim is supported by binding energy calculations comparing different mutations.

claim: AITC enhanced typical TRPA1 currents in cells expressing WT mTRPA1-mCherry or the V780A, F786A, L850A and Y852A mutants.
source: AITC (300 µM) enhanced typical TRPA1 currents in cells expressing WT mTRPA1-mCherry or the V780A, F786A, L850A and Y852A mutants (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings shown in Figure 7.

claim: All AITC-induced currents were blocked by the TRPA1 antagonist HC030031.
source: All AITC-induced currents were blocked by the TRPA1 antagonist HC030031 (100 µM) (Figure 7A,B and Figure 7—figure supplement 1A,B,C)
evidence: The claim is supported by whole-cell patch-clamp recordings showing current blockade by HC030031.

claim: The current increase strongly correlated with the amplitude of the Ca2+ responses (R = 0.94).
source: These results are fully consistent with the above-described Ca2+ imaging measurements, as the current increase strongly correlated with the amplitude of the Ca2+ responses (Figure 7D; R = 0.94)
evidence: The claim is supported by correlation analysis between current and calcium response data shown in Figure 7D.

claim: WT mTRPA1-mCherry channels were rather evenly distributed at the membrane in control conditions.
source: WT channels were rather evenly distributed at the membrane in the control condition (Figure 8A)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images shown in Figure 8A.

claim: MCD treatment resulted in clustered localization of WT mTRPA1-mCherry at the plasma membrane.
source: In contrast, cells treated with MCD showed a clustered localization at the plasma membrane, significant amplitude reduction across the cell and strong retention in aggregates underneath the plasma membrane that relates to an ~75% lower amplitude at the plasma membrane (Figure 8B)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 8B.

claim: The V780A, F786A, L850A and Y852A mutants displayed altered distribution at the plasma membrane in control conditions, similar to WT in MCD-treated cells.
source: Interestingly, the V780A, F786A, L850A and Y852A mutants displayed altered distribution already in control condition, with features similar to those found for WT in MCD-treated cells (Figure 8C,E,H)
evidence: The claim is supported by confocal microscopy images and quantification shown in Figure 8.

claim: MCD treatment failed to reduce the total mCherry signal and the mCherry fraction at the plasma membrane for all mutants except L850A.
source: The MCD treatment failed to reduce the total mCherry signal and the mCherry fraction at the plasma membrane for all mutants except L850A (Figure 8G,H)
evidence: The claim is supported by quantification of confocal microscopy data shown in Figure 8.

claim: Mutations in TRPA1 leading to defective interactions with cholesterol interfere with the pattern of localization of the channel at the plasma membrane.
source: Taken together, these data indicate that mutations in TRPA1 leading to defective interactions with cholesterol also interfere with the pattern of localization of the channel at the plasma membrane
evidence: The claim is inferred from the confocal microscopy data showing altered localization patterns in mutants.

claim: Several TRP channels have been found to be segregated in lipid rafts, including TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC4 and TRPC5.
source: Several TRP channels have been found to be segregated in lipid rafts. These include members of the TRPC subfamily (TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC4 and TRPC5) (Ambudkar et al., 2004; Lockwich et al., 2000; Brownlow and Sage, 2005; Graziani et al., 2006)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: TRPV1 has been found to be segregated in lipid rafts.
source: Several TRP channels have been found to be segregated in lipid rafts. These include members of the TRPC subfamily (TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC4 and TRPC5) (Ambudkar et al., 2004; Lockwich et al., 2000; Brownlow and Sage, 2005; Graziani et al., 2006) and the sensory channels TRPV1 (Szoke et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRPV4 has been found to be segregated in lipid rafts.
source: Several TRP channels have been found to be segregated in lipid rafts. These include members of the TRPC subfamily (TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC4 and TRPC5) (Ambudkar et al., 2004; Lockwich et al., 2000; Brownlow and Sage, 2005; Graziani et al., 2006) and the sensory channels TRPV1 (Szoke et al., 2010), TRPV4 (Kumari et al., 2015)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: TRPM8 has been found to be segregated in lipid rafts.
source: Several TRP channels have been found to be segregated in lipid rafts. These include members of the TRPC subfamily (TRPC1, TRPC3, TRPC4 and TRPC5) (Ambudkar et al., 2004; Lockwich et al., 2000; Brownlow and Sage, 2005; Graziani et al., 2006) and the sensory channels TRPV1 (Szoke et al., 2010), TRPV4 (Kumari et al., 2015) and TRPM8 (Morenilla-Palao et al., 2009)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: SMase induces breakdown of sphingolipids into ceramide, which partially displaces cholesterol from lipid rafts.
source: SMase induces breakdown of sphingolipids into ceramide, which partially displace cholesterol from the lipid rafts (Megha and London, 2004; Yu et al., 2005) and leads to the formation of ceramide enriched domains (De Tullio et al., 2008)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Sphingolipids make up 30% of total lipids in myelin sheets of neurons and oligodendrocytes.
source: For instance, sphingolipids are a minor component in erythrocytes, but are particularly abundant in neurons and oligodendrocytes, where they make up 30% of total lipids in myelin sheets (Ogawa-Goto and Abe, 1998; Buccoliero and Futerman, 2003)
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of TRPV4.
source: Several mammalian sensory TRP channels (TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPM3 and TRPM8) and the Drosophila photoreceptor TRP-like channel (dTRPL) are sensitive to modification of the cholesterol content at the plasma membrane. However, they are distinctly regulated, as cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of TRPV4 (Lakk et al., 2017) and dTRPL (Peters et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of dTRPL.
source: Several mammalian sensory TRP channels (TRPV1, TRPV4, TRPM3 and TRPM8) and the Drosophila photoreceptor TRP-like channel (dTRPL) are sensitive to modification of the cholesterol content at the plasma membrane. However, they are distinctly regulated, as cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of TRPV4 (Lakk et al., 2017) and dTRPL (Peters et al., 2017)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol depletion enhances stimulation of TRPM8.
source: However, they are distinctly regulated, as cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of TRPV4 (Lakk et al., 2017) and dTRPL (Peters et al., 2017), but enhances stimulation of TRPM8 (Morenilla-Palao et al., 2009) and TRPM3 (Naylor et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Cholesterol depletion enhances stimulation of TRPM3.
source: However, they are distinctly regulated, as cholesterol depletion reduces the activation of TRPV4 (Lakk et al., 2017) and dTRPL (Peters et al., 2017), but enhances stimulation of TRPM8 (Morenilla-Palao et al., 2009) and TRPM3 (Naylor et al., 2010)
evidence: The claim is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: Extracellular MCD treatment decreased the maximal response of mTRPA1 channels to AITC.
source: We found that the treatment with extracellular MCD decreased the maximal response of mTRPA1 channels to AITC, which can be readily explained by the reduced channel expression at the plasma membrane (Figure 7)
evidence: The claim is supported by functional data and confocal microscopy showing reduced membrane expression.

claim: Extracellular MCD treatment strongly reduced the sensitivity of TRPA1 to chemical stimulation with AITC (a 5-fold increased EC50).
